prompt: Why do plane-wave codes like VASP describe orbitals as a sum of waves?

options.text: Waves of fixed wavelength form a simple, systematic basis: more waves give a better answer, and nothing depends on where the atoms are
options.why: That is the key advantage: one number, the cutoff, controls the quality for every atom type.

options.text: Because electrons in crystals really are free plane waves
options.why: Tempting, but the orbitals are not free waves. The waves are only a convenient set of building blocks.

options.text: Because plane waves need no pseudopotential
options.why: The reverse: plane waves need a smooth potential, which is why pseudopotentials are used.

prompt: In a plane-wave calculation, which waves are kept in the basis?

options.text: Those whose kinetic energy is at most the cutoff
options.why: The cutoff sets a maximum kinetic energy; every wave below it is included.

options.text: Those whose wavelength is exactly the cell length
options.why: Only a few waves would fit that rule, and the basis would be far too small.

options.text: Those that overlap an atom
options.why: The basis does not depend on atom positions; all waves under the cutoff are kept.

hints: The cutoff is an energy.
Waves with larger wave vector have more kinetic energy.

options.text: It becomes four times larger
options.why: Halving the wavelength doubles k, and the energy goes as k squared.

options.text: It becomes twice as large
options.why: Energy is proportional to k squared, not k.

options.text: It stays the same
options.why: Shorter waves are more strongly curved, so they carry more kinetic energy.

hints: Wavelength and k are inversely related: k = 2 pi / wavelength.

prompt: What does a higher ENCUT do to a calculation?

options.text: Includes more plane waves: the result gets more accurate and the run gets slower
options.why: It is a straight trade of cost for accuracy, until the result stops changing.

options.text: Makes the SCF loop converge faster
options.why: The cutoff changes the basis, not the mixing, so convergence speed is not what it controls.

options.text: Moves the Fermi level
options.why: The Fermi level is set by the electrons and bands, not by the size of the basis.

hints: ENCUT is the largest kinetic energy included.
Larger set of waves means more work.

prompt: If ENCUT is not set, what does VASP use?

options.text: The largest ENMAX among the POTCAR files
options.why: VASP reads a recommended minimum from each POTCAR and takes the largest.

options.text: A fixed 500 eV
options.why: There is no single universal default; it depends on the elements.

options.text: Zero, which means no basis
options.why: VASP always needs a cutoff; it chooses one from the POTCAR files.

prompt: For a run that changes the cell shape or volume, what does the author's rule recommend for ENCUT?

options.text: About 1.3 times the largest ENMAX
options.why: Changing the cell changes the basis, which causes Pulay stress; a higher cutoff reduces it.

options.text: Exactly the largest ENMAX
options.why: That is fine for fixed-cell runs, but a cell relaxation needs more.

options.text: Half of the largest ENMAX
options.why: Too low a cutoff makes the stress wrong, not just the energy.

hints: A higher cutoff reduces the Pulay error.
The factor is bigger than 1.

prompt: What does Bloch's theorem say about an electron orbital in a perfect crystal?

options.text: It is a plane wave multiplied by a function that repeats with the lattice
options.why: That is why each orbital is labelled by a wave vector k plus a band number.

options.text: It is the same on every atom, with no variation
options.why: The repeating part can vary a lot within the cell; only its repetition is fixed.

options.text: It is localized on a single atom
options.why: Bloch states spread over the whole crystal.

hints: Think about a wave modulated by the crystal's pattern.

prompt: Why does a VASP run need a set of k-points, rather than one calculation?

options.text: Quantities such as the density are averages over all k in the Brillouin zone, and the average is approximated by a finite sample
options.why: The sum over an infinite crystal becomes a sum over a few chosen k.

options.text: Each k-point is a different atom
options.why: k labels waves in reciprocal space, not atoms.

options.text: Each k-point is a separate ionic step
options.why: k-points are sampled within one SCF step, not across the relaxation.

hints: The crystal is effectively infinite.
The density is an integral over k.

prompt: You double the k-mesh density and the energy changes by 5 meV per atom. What should you conclude?

options.text: The first mesh was not converged; test a denser one until the change is below your tolerance

options.text: The first mesh was fine, since the change is small
options.why: 5 meV per atom is above the usual 1 meV target, so the first mesh is not yet converged.

options.text: The second mesh must be wrong
options.why: A denser mesh is not wrong; it is closer to the limit.

prompt: A cell is long in one direction. Which k-mesh is sensible along that direction?

options.text: Fewer k-points, because the reciprocal cell is short in that direction
options.why: Real-space length and reciprocal length are inverse, so long cells need fewer points.

options.text: More k-points, since the cell is big
options.why: The reverse: a long direction means a short reciprocal direction.

options.text: The same number as the short directions
options.why: That wastes work; spacing in k, not the count, should be similar.

prompt: What is the first Brillouin zone?

options.text: The Wigner-Seitz cell of the reciprocal lattice: the region closer to the origin than to any other reciprocal lattice point
options.why: It is the standard unit cell of reciprocal space.

options.text: The Wigner-Seitz cell of the real-space lattice
options.why: That is the real-space version; the Brillouin zone lives in reciprocal space.

options.text: The set of all occupied states
options.why: Occupation is a separate idea; the zone is a region of wave vectors.

hints: It is built like a Wigner-Seitz cell.
It lives in reciprocal space.

prompt: If you make the real-space cell larger, what happens to the Brillouin zone?

options.text: It becomes smaller
options.why: Reciprocal lengths go as the inverse of real lengths.

options.text: It becomes larger
options.why: The relation is inverse, so a bigger cell gives a smaller zone.

options.text: It does not change
options.why: The zone depends on the lattice; scaling the lattice scales the zone.

Big in real space means small in reciprocal space.

prompt: Why can we restrict the wave vector k to the first Brillouin zone?

options.text: Any k outside it differs from one inside by a reciprocal lattice vector, and describes the same Bloch state
options.why: The zone contains one copy of every distinct state.

options.text: Wave vectors outside it are unphysical
options.why: They are not wrong; they are equivalent copies of states already inside.

options.text: The electrons cannot move outside it
options.why: The zone is about wave vectors, not positions.

hints: Shifting k by a reciprocal lattice vector changes nothing.

prompt: How does a Gamma-centred mesh differ from a Monkhorst-Pack mesh?

options.text: A Gamma-centred mesh always includes the Gamma point; Monkhorst-Pack with an even number of divisions does not
options.why: For odd divisions the two coincide, for even ones the Monkhorst-Pack mesh is shifted off Gamma.

options.text: Gamma-centred meshes have fewer points in total
options.why: The point counts are the same for the same divisions.

options.text: They sample different physical quantities
options.why: Both sample the same integral; they only differ in where the points sit.

hints: Look at the even-division case.

options.text: A single k-point

prompt: Why test k-mesh and cutoff convergence separately?

options.text: They control different approximations: the basis size and the sampling of the zone
options.why: Each can limit accuracy independently, so each needs its own convergence test.

options.text: They are the same tag under two names
options.why: They are different settings: ENCUT and the k-mesh.

options.text: One of them has no effect on energy
options.why: Both change the energy; both must be converged.

prompt: What is the purpose of smearing in a metal calculation?

options.text: To replace the sharp step in occupation at the Fermi level with a smooth one, which helps the k-sum and the SCF loop converge
options.why: A smooth step is easier to integrate with a limited number of k-points.

options.text: To make the metal hotter in a physically exact way
options.why: Only Fermi-Dirac smearing corresponds to a physical temperature, and the others are numerical aids.

options.text: To remove the Fermi level
options.why: The Fermi level remains; only the step at it is blurred.

hints: Think about what is hard about a sharp step.
It is mostly a numerical aid.

options.why: The gap gives a range of valid values, so the exact position is not fixed by the electron count.

options.text: Metals have no electrons
options.why: Metals have many electrons at the Fermi level.

options.text: Insulators have no bands
options.why: Insulators have bands with a gap between them.
